claims.text: The mechanical and thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys at high temperature is governed by the formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates enhance high-temperature strength and stability.
The proposed strengthening and stabilization arise from solid-solution strengthening, precipitation hardening, and grain-boundary pinning.
The relevant initial alloy may have either an FCC or BCC crystal structure.
In situ neutron diffraction and HRTEM will be used at 800–1200 °C with a heating rate of 10 °C/min and a one-hour hold.
The applicable mechanical conditions are 100–500 MPa at a strain rate of 10^-4 s^-1.
The governing precipitates are coherent and 10–50 nm in size.
The governing precipitates have a volume fraction of 0.1–0.5.
Formation of the coherent precipitate structure produces precipitation hardening.
Formation of the coherent precipitate structure produces grain-boundary pinning.
Formation of the coherent precipitate structure produces solid-solution strengthening.
Relative to an alloy without coherent nanoscale precipitates, the precipitate-containing alloy will have a 20–50% higher yield strength.
Relative to an alloy without coherent nanoscale precipitates, the precipitate-containing alloy will have a 10–30% lower thermal expansion coefficient.
The baseline alloy has a yield strength of 500 MPa.
The baseline alloy has a thermal expansion coefficient of 10^-5 K^-1.
A comparison between alloys with and without coherent nanoscale precipitates can isolate the precipitate structure as the governing cause.
A lack of statistically significant differences in both yield strength and thermal expansion coefficient would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The rule describes results as 'not significantly different' while specifying p < 0.05, which conventionally indicates a statistically significant difference. A nonsignificance rule would ordinarily use p >= 0.05, subject to an adequately powered equivalence or noninferiority design.
